sections.h1:
Irreversible actions deserve
better interfaces than this.
sections.lead: Design for wallets, exchanges, and onchain products — where a mistyped address is permanent and the interface is the only safety net the user has.

sections.body: Radiant designs wallets, onchain products, and crypto brands: transaction and signing flows, onboarding without seed-phrase panic, portfolio and trading interfaces, and sites that explain a protocol to people outside it. sections.label: Web3 & Crypto
sections.challenge: Your onboarding asks a newcomer to write down twelve words and understand gas before they have done anything useful. Signing requests show a hash and ask for trust. Everything is irreversible, nothing is explained in advance, and the people you most want to reach are exactly the ones the interface filters out.

cta.text: Talk to us about your onchain project

sections.heading: What we fix in onchain products

cards.title: Onboarding that frightens newcomers off
cards.body: Seed phrases, gas, and networks presented in the first sixty seconds. We sequence the scary parts after first value, and design recovery that does not depend on a screenshot in someone's camera roll.

cards.title: Signing requests nobody can read
cards.body: If the user cannot tell what they are approving, they are gambling. We design transaction previews in plain language: what moves, to whom, what it costs, and what it cannot be undone from.

cards.title: Brands that trade credibility for hype
cards.body: Neon gradients and anonymous mascots make a serious protocol look like a rug. We design identities that read as financial infrastructure, because increasingly that is what they are.

sections.heading:
What onchain teams need,
by stage.

steps.label: Protocol
steps.title: Explain the mechanism
steps.body: Documentation, a site, and visual explanations that make the protocol legible to developers, investors, and press without resorting to jargon or promises.

steps.label: Product
steps.title: Design the irreversible moments
steps.body: Wallet connection, signing, bridging, and recovery — the four places users lose money. Everything else can be iterated; these have to be right at launch.

steps.label: Scale
steps.title: Reach beyond crypto-native users
steps.body: Fiat on-ramps, account abstraction, and language that assumes no prior knowledge, for the audience that will never read a block explorer.

cards.title: How do you design onboarding without scaring people?
cards.body: Let people do something useful before custody becomes their problem, explain each irreversible step at the moment it happens, and offer recovery options that match how real people store secrets.

cards.title: How do you make transactions understandable?
cards.body: Translate the call data into a sentence: what leaves the wallet, what arrives, what it costs, and what permission is being granted indefinitely. Approval scope is where most losses start.

cards.title: Can you design for both crypto-native and new users?
cards.body: Yes, by layering: a simple default path with the advanced controls available but not in the way. Trying to serve both in one undifferentiated interface serves neither.

cards.title: Do you work with pre-launch and stealth protocols?
cards.body: Yes, under NDA. A good deal of onchain work happens before a token or mainnet launch, and we treat timing as confidential.

cards.title: Do you design token or marketing material?
cards.body: We design brand, site, and product. We do not write or design anything that promises returns, and we will push back on claims that read as financial advice.

cards.title: Can you work with our smart contract constraints?
cards.body: Yes. We ask your engineers in week one what is on-chain, what is indexed, and what is slow — those constraints shape the interface more than any visual decision.

sections.challenge: Show us your connect-and-sign path. We will tell you where a careful user hesitates and where a careless one loses money.
